scenario: AITA for pulling a sickie so I can go to a job interview? | TL;DR at the end I work as a nurse in a community hospital. When I first started working there, I absolutely loved it. However, due to various site closures, we've basically become a 'dumping ground' for patients who can't go home, but can't stay in hospital. I was mostly fine with it, as we were a palliative/end of life (EOL) unit with patients who had complex health issues. Now, we're basically a free care home. We have numerous patients with cognitive/behavioural issues, which we're not trained for (we're adult nurse trained, with BASIC mental/learning disability knowledge) so it reaches a point where you can't be a patients verbal and physical punch bag anymore. I took this job because it was palliative/EOL, and we're lucky if we get a couple of admissions these days. My boss is also awful. She's always been blunt with her staff, which at first I respected, because at least you knew where you stood. Now, she will pick at anything for an excuse to tell at you. Her complaints over the last few months have gotten even more cutting and demoralising; a few prime examples are complaining we don't 'use our initiative' however as soon as we do, she tells us it's wrong. She's accused us of 'killing patients' by not offering our EOL patients food (they're basically comatose, have no swallow, and would likely die from choking rather than their actual condition) and she tried to report me for a drug error that wasn't actually wrong. It wasn't until the medical team AND THE PEOPLE WHO WROTE THE GUIDELINES ON THE Drug told her that I was right, she backed down. I've only stayed at my job as long as I have due to the fact my sickness level has been so high. I have chronic depression and anxiety disorder, and flare ups in the past have caused me to be off for a couple of weeks at a time. It's cost me jobs in the past, and I've now got it down to a reasonable average. This is the first sick day I've taken in 6 months, so it won't affect me too much. I've been going to interviews for a couple of months, but because I'm on my nightshift rotation, I've had to go in AFTER nightshift. Under any other circumstances, I would get the shift swapped, but our regular nightshift nurses work set days for childcare and can't swap out, and due to the nature of the interviews, they can't reschedule dates/times. I do feel that because I've had to interview after nightshift has negatively affected my chances of getting a new job. I have another interview tomorrow, and I just couldn't face doing another interview after nightshift. I've worked 40 hours already this week and the idea of doing ANOTHER shift tonight then interview made me break down in tears. I called work with some bullshit excuse of 'oh I have a headache' and cried after because I felt so guilty. So, Reddit. AITA? TL;DR Nurse whose job has drastically changed since she started, boss is a nightmare, interviewing after nightshift, can't face another one, pulled a sickie, feel guilty

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently while keeping the festive spirit alive: ### **1. Clean & Prep the House (Most Important First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, dining area, entrance). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and storage spaces. - **Launder bedding, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least dust them). - **Wash windows/mirrors** for a bright, welcoming look. - *Why?* A clean home feels sacred and ready for guests—it’s the foundation for decorations. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decorative Lights)** - **Place diyas** in key areas: - **Entrance** (mandatory for Diwali—use a small table or wall-mounted holder). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Dining area** (if space allows). - **Balcony/porch** (if you have one). - **Use LED string lights** for a modern touch (safe and energy-efficient). - **Marigold garlands** (traditional) or **fairy lights** (for a soft glow). - *Tip:* If short on time, focus on the **entrance and living room** first—they make the biggest impact. ### **3. Quick Decor Updates (Minimal Effort, Big Impact)** - **Hang rangoli** (even a simple design at the entrance or near diyas). - **Place small decorative items**: - **Diwali-themed candles** (scented ones add ambiance). - **Mini statues** (Ganesha, Lakshmi, or lotus motifs). - **Fresh flowers** (marigolds or jasmine for a natural touch). - **Swap out throw pillows/blankets** for festive colors (gold, red, or orange). ### **4. Final Touches (Last-Minute)** - **Set up a small altar** (if you observe puja) with diyas, flowers, and incense. - **Arrange snacks/drinks** in a pretty tray (for guests). - **Test all lights** (diyas, bulbs, etc.) to avoid last-minute issues. - **Spritz air fresheners** (sandalwood or rose-scented) for a fresh feel. ### **5. Day Before Diwali (Quick Checklist)** - **Replenish diyas** (if using oil-based ones). - **Charge phone/laptop** (for photos/videos). - **Set out guest seating** (if hosting). - **Prepare a welcome note** (on the door or entrance). --- ### **Time-Saving Tips:** ✅ **DIY shortcuts**: - Use **glow sticks** (cheap and safe) as temporary diyas. - **Paint rocks** with gold paint for instant decor. - **Buy pre-made rangoli stencils** or use chalk for quick designs. ✅ **Delegate**: - Ask a family member to handle **lighting** while you focus on **cleaning**. - If you have kids, let them help with **hanging garlands or placing small diyas**. ✅ **Skip perfection**: - A few well-placed diyas + a clean entrance look **far more festive** than half-decorated rooms. --- ### **Sample Timeline (If You’re Short on Time):** - **Day 1 (Today)**: Clean + place diyas in entrance/living room. - **Day 2**: Add rangoli, garlands, and small decor items. - **Day 3 (Before Diwali)**: Final touches (lights, snacks, altar). --- **Most important priority?** **Cleanliness + entrance diyas**—they set the tone for guests. The rest can be layered in gradually. Wishing you a joyful Diwali! 🪔✨

However: - **If you see this as a one-time "emergency"**, it’s **understandable**. - **If you see it as a pattern**, it becomes **self-sabotaging**. **Ask yourself:** - **Could I have handled this differently?** (E.g., escalated to HR, used a doctor’s note, or left earlier.) - **What’s the worst that could happen?** (E.g., being fired—would you have a backup plan?) - **What’s the best that could happen?** (E.g., getting a better job—would this sick day help or hurt that?) --- ### **Alternative Actions to Consider** If you’re **not ready to quit but need a break**, try: 1. **Framing it as a "mental health day"**: - Call in "sick" but **leave a message** explaining you’re **temporarily unwell** (not lying, but not admitting burnout). - Follow up with a **doctor’s note** if you can (even a short-term one). 2. **Negotiating a temporary leave**: - Say: *"I’m struggling with [anxiety/depression] and need a few days to recover. Can we discuss a short leave?"* 3. **Documenting workplace issues**: - If your boss is **actively harmful**, write down **specific incidents** (e.g., drug error accusation) and **save emails/messages**. This could help if you **leave or escalate to HR**. 4. **Looking for a "bridge job"**: - If you can’t leave immediately, find a **short-term role** (e.g., agency nursing) to **buy time** while you job hunt. --- ### **TL;DR Verdict: It’s Complicated** - **Not "wrong"** if: - You’re at a **genuine breaking point**. - You **pair it with a plan** (e.g., resigning, applying to better jobs). - You **minimize the lie** (e.g., don’t say "headache" if you’re actually exhausted—be vague). - **Risky if**: - You **repeat this pattern** (could lead to job loss). - Your boss **retaliates** (some toxic managers punish "sickies" harshly). - You **don’t have a backup job lined up**. **Final Thought:** You’re **not obligated to stay in a toxic, unsustainable job**—but **burning bridges** (even via sick leave) can **limit your options later**. If this job is **actively harming your health**, the **greater "wrong"** might be **staying**. Would you consider **quitting immediately** (with a doctor’s note) instead of calling in sick? That might be the **cleanest exit**—but it depends on your financial/emotional readiness. --- **You’re not alone in this.** Nursing is one of the most **exploited professions**, and **workplace toxicity + mental health struggles** are a **real crisis**.
